sites.name: Alpha Mine
sites.componentDetail: Historic silver mine locality on the Alpha-Corsair vein system
overview: The Alpha Mine marks one of the earliest documented silver discoveries in the Creede area. Silver was found here in 1869, two decades before the district's famous boom, but the complex ore could not then be treated profitably.

Later geological work places the mine in the Alpha-Corsair vein system on the west side of the Creede graben. That structure was mined for silver before 1910 and has been studied for its distinctive lead-isotope signature and potential early gold-bearing mineralization.

timeline.text: Silver was discovered at the Alpha Mine, but the complex ore could not be processed profitably with the methods then available.
USGS-supported research records silver mining on the Alpha-Corsair vein system before 1910.
A USGS-authored study reported that galena from the Alpha-Corsair structure had an isotopic signature resembling early gold-stage mineralization in the North Amethyst system.

moreHistory: The Alpha discovery predates the rich Willow Creek finds that triggered Creede's boom beginning in 1889, making it an important early chapter in the district's mining history.
USGS Mineral Resources Data System information identifies Alpha as a Creede-district silver mine, with zinc, antimony, copper and lead also recorded.
The mapped point near 37.8450, -106.9625 is a historical mine locality rather than a field-surveyed surviving opening. Visitors should not assume that an accessible portal remains at the point.

sourceReferences.title: USGS — Lead isotope compositions as guides to early gold mineralization: The North Amethyst vein system, Creede district, Colorado
Colorado Geological Survey OF-99-18 — Selected mines near Creede

sites.name: Antelope Warm Spring
sites.componentDetail: Geothermal spring, concrete-lined cistern, and documented former swimming-pool system
overview: Antelope Warm Spring is a documented low-temperature geothermal spring in Mineral County. Colorado Geological Survey records place it near 37.74333, -107.03722 and measured water near 32°C (about 90°F) during 1975 sampling.

A 1993 state field visit found the spring issuing into a concrete-lined cistern beside a wooden building containing a swimming pool. The spring water had historically been used to fill that pool, linking the natural feature to a small recreation structure.

timeline.text: Colorado geothermal investigators sampled Antelope Warm Spring and recorded water near 32°C.
The spring's location and water chemistry were published in the Colorado Geological Survey's statewide thermal-water inventory.
A Colorado Geological Survey field visit documented a concrete-lined cistern and a nearby building containing a spring-fed swimming pool.

moreHistory: The 1993 survey described the cistern as roughly 6 by 4 feet at ground level and about 5 feet deep, about 20 feet north of the pool building.
USGS later included Antelope Warm Spring in its inventory of fluorine and thermal waters in central Colorado, retaining the same mapped locality.

The mapped point identifies the documented spring and historic pool setting, not a guarantee of present public access, bathing conditions, or surviving structures. Visitors should observe current ownership, signs and closures.

sourceReferences.title: Colorado Geological Survey IS-06 — Hydrogeological Data of Thermal Springs and Wells in Colorado
Colorado Geological Survey OF-95-01 — Results of the 1992–1993 Low-Temperature Geothermal Assessment Program
USGS SIR 2010-5113 — Fluorine, Fluorite, and Fluorspar in Central Colorado

sites.name: Bird Creek Mine
sites.location: Bird Creek, southeast of Spar City
sites.componentDetail: Historic tunnel working with a documented 222-foot raise
overview: The Bird Creek Mine is a small historic working in Mineral County's Royal Arch–Spar City district, along Bird Creek southeast of Spar City. Federal mineral records associate the property with silver, lead and zinc and identify the Per Cent No. 12 and No. 15 claims.

The recorded workings include a tunnel driven generally southeast and a 222-foot raise. The area was prospected intermittently from the early 1900s, but thick soil, forest cover, landslides and glacial deposits made systematic exploration difficult.

timeline.text: Prospecting began in the Bird Creek area and continued intermittently.
Federal mineral records list the Bird Creek Mining Company of Creede as the property owner.
USGS Geologic Quadrangle Map GQ-1052 documented the geology of the Spar City quadrangle surrounding the mine.

moreHistory: The mine lies near the southern extension of the Deep Creek graben within the Creede caldera volcanic field, where minor faults helped localize mineralization.
Sphalerite is recorded as an ore mineral and barite as gangue. The amount of production, if any, was considered unknown and probably small in the federal record.

The mapped point near 37.69806, -106.94833 identifies the documented Bird Creek tunnel locality. It is not a field survey of present access or portal condition; visitors should respect landownership, closures and mine hazards.

sourceReferences.title: USGS — Geologic map of the Spar City quadrangle, Mineral County, Colorado
USGS Professional Paper 475-D — Geologic setting of the Spar City district
USGS MRDS-derived Bird Creek Mine record

sites.name: Amethyst Mine
sites.location: West Willow Creek north of Creede, Creede Mining District
overview: The Amethyst Mine was one of the largest and richest historic producers in the Creede Mining District, developed on the Amethyst vein along West Willow Creek north of Creede.
Mining began during Creede's 1891 silver boom, and published state and federal histories document major silver, gold, lead, and zinc production along with extensive underground development.

timeline.text: N. C. Creede located the Amethyst lode in 1891; the mine began producing during the opening year of the Creede boom.
By the end of 1892, published federal history reported roughly 20,000 tons of ore produced with an estimated value of about $2 million.
Colorado Geological Survey's compiled mine history reports 7,480 tons produced in 1899, containing substantial silver, gold, and lead.
The mine closed in 1911, then was leased in 1912 to the Creede Triune Mining Company, which opened new stopes and returned the mill to operation.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey records describe the Amethyst Mine about two miles north of Creede near West Willow Creek and Nelson Creek. The property was first developed by two shafts on the Amethyst vein and later through the Amethyst No. 5 Tunnel near West Willow Creek.

Federal mine history places the Amethyst on the steep slope of Bachelor Mountain between the Last Chance and Happy Thought mines and documents amethystine quartz carrying rich gold and silver near the outcrop.

The mapped identification point near 37.8850, -106.93722 is retained from the USGS Mineral Resources Data System-derived Amethyst Mine record as a defensible site-level reference. It is not presented as a field-surveyed surviving shaft collar, portal, property boundary, or statement of current access.
